Original Research
Do certain blood groups increase COVID-19 severity and mortality?
Tegene Atamenta kitaw *, Ribka Nigatu Haile
Department of Nursing, College of Health Science, Woldia University, Woldia, Ethiopia
ARTICLE INFO
Keywords:
ABO blood types
COVID-19 severity
Mortality
ABSTRACT
Background: The existence of a relationship between the ABO blood group and COVID-19 severity and mortality 
is still an unresolved concern. Some studies report that groups O and A show a lower and higher risk of 
developing severe COVID-19 and mortality, respectively. Some studies also report the reverse. There are 
inconclusive results from different studies. Thus, this study sought to determine the possible associations of ABO 
blood type with COVID-19 severity and mortality.
Methods: A retrospective study was conducted among 570 adults with real-time reverse transcription-polymerase 
chain reaction confirmed positive COVID-19 patients attending Eka Kotebe General Hospital, COVID-19 Treatment Center. A Kaplan-Meier survival curve was computed to examine the difference in survival experience 
between ABO blood groups. Multinomial and binary logistic regression models were fitted to determine the 
association between ABO blood group with COVID-19 severity and mortality, respectively.
Result: 238 (41.8 %) COVID-19 patients had blood group B, followed by 201 (35.3 %) A, 82 (14.4 %) O, and 49 
(8.6 %) AB blood type. 23.68 % of participants develop severe COVID-19. Overall, 15.26 % COVID-19-related 
mortality was found. No difference in survival experience was observed between ABO blood types. There was 
no statistically significant association between ABO blood type and COVID-19 severity, and mortality.
Conclusion: We found no relationship between ABO blood group differences and COVID-19 severity, and mortality. Further, well-design-controlled studies are suggested to explore the potential link of ABO blood group with 
COVID-19 severity and mortality.
Introduction
In December 2019, from China, Wuhan, Hubei Province, pneumonialike symptomatic individuals create an alarm to the world. Later on,

those individuals were diagnosed with coronavirus diseases (COVID19). Coronavirus is named after its crown-like shape [1]. On January 7, 
2020, Chinese researchers started isolating a new individual infected by 
a coronavirus. On March 11, 2020, WHO announced that the emerging 
coronavirus (COVID-19) disease was a global pandemic. Coronavirus 
(COVID-19) is a respiratory tract disease caused by a newly occurring 
coronavirus species called SARS-CoV2 [2]. So far, COVID-19 has 
covered more than 218 countries and territories, with over 763 million 
confirmed cases and over 6.9 million deaths reported globally [3].
As several studies revealed that preexisting comorbidities such as 
diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, kidney diseases and 
chronic neurological disorders might have a relationship with COVID-19 
severity and mortality [4–6] Furthermore, some laboratory markers 
were also reported as they have a relationship with COVID-19 severity 
and mortality. An increase from baseline of creatine kinase, CRP, white 
blood cell, D-dimer, raised ALT (alanine transaminase) and AST 
(Aspartate Transaminase), increased cardiac troponin, and elevated 
LDH, decrease in albumin, and decrease in lymphocyte account were all 
associated with severity and higher mortality rate [7,8].
Recent emerging studies have urged that there is a relationship between the ABO blood group and COVID-19 severity and mortality. Patients with blood type A/AB had a higher mortality rate than those with 
O/B (32 % vs. 18.5 %). Patients with blood type O/B had a lower risk of 
intubation than patients with blood type A/AB (49.2 % vs. 52 %) [9]. A 
study done in Canada revealed that COVID-19 patients with blood 
groups A or AB are at increased risk of requiring mechanical ventilation 
compared to those with blood group O or B. Patients with blood group A 
or AB appear to show greater disease severity than patients with blood 
group O or B [10].
Similarly, other systematic review studies reveal that blood group A

individuals’ vulnerability to COVID-19 and blood type AB confer a lower 
risk of SARS-COV-2 severity [11–13]. In another study in India, patients

with blood group O had a lower mortality risk, while blood group B 
increased COVID-19 mortality [14]. A systematic review of studies 
suggests that individuals of blood group A are at a higher risk of infection with SARS-CoV-2 and may develop severe COVID-19 outcomes, 
whereas blood group O is considered protective against bad outcomes 
[15]. In contrast a study in Mexico revealed quite different findings, 
asserting that patients with blood group A are less likely to die from 
COVID-19 than those with blood group O [16].
Having the above disagreed finding, several studies also demonstrate 
no association between the ABO blood group and COVID-19 severity or 
mortality [17–21].
Despite the above findings, controversy remains over whether there 
is a relationship between ABO blood group and COVID-19 severity and 
mortality. Which blood type is associated with poor outcomes or is 
protective. Thus, this study sought to determine the possible association 
of ABO blood group with COVID-19 severity and mortality.
Methods
Study design, data sources and setting
A retrospective study was conducted among 570 adults’ real-time 
reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) confirmed

positive COVID-19 patients. The primary data for this study was previously published [22]. The study was conducted at Eka Kotebe General 
Hospital, a COVID-19 treatment center. The hospital was the first 
COVID-19 treatment center in Ethiopia. The Center is located in Addis 
Abeba, Ethiopia’s capital city, where more COVID-19 cases have been 
reported than in any other Ethiopian town. The Center was relatively the 
only well-equipped treatment facility with a ventilator machine, access 
to the COVID-19 diagnostic test, and qualified medical staff.
Population
Adults (≥18 years) confirmed positive SARS-COV-2 with RT-PCR 
were included. Wear as incomplete patient chart (unknown ABO blood 
group status) were excluded from the study.
Definitions
The severity of COVID-19 was classified as follows: [1] Asymptomatic infection: individuals who test positive for SARSCoV-2 using a 
virologic test but who have no symptoms that are consistent with 
COVID-19; [2] mild illness: individuals who have any of the various 
signs and symptoms of COVID-19 (e.g., fever, cough, sore throat, malaise, headache, muscle pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, loss of taste 
and smell) but who do not have shortness of breath, dyspnea, or 
abnormal chest imaging; [3] moderate illness: individuals who show

breaths per minute, or lung infiltrates involving more than 50 % of the 
lung fields [23,24].
Data processing and analysis
A total of 570 study participants with known ABO blood groups were 
extracted. The data was coded, cleaned, and edited. Analysis was done 
using STATA version 17 software. Descriptive statistics are analyzed and 
presented in terms of frequency and percentage. Variance inflation 
factor (VIF) and tolerance were computed to check the existence of 
multicollinearity. If the VIF is above four, multicollinearity might exist 
[25–29]. In this study, the maximum VIF was 1.21, with a mean VIF of 
1.09. Thus, there is no multicollinearity between covariates. A Chisquare test was computed to compare the characteristics of the patients related to COVID-19 severity and morality. Hosmer–Lemeshow 
goodness-of-fit test was computed to test the model fitness and found that 
the p-value is 0.8, indicating a good logistic regression model fit. 
Multinomial and binary logistic regression models were fitted to determine the association between ABO blood group with COVID-19 severity 
and mortality, respectively. Furthermore, multivariable analysis was 
done to examine their relationship.
Results
Baseline characteristics of COVID-19 patients
The median age of the participants was 42 years (IQR, 28–60). The 
majority were male (63 %), and 20 % of the patients had both hypertension and diabetes as comorbid conditions. The most common comorbid illnesses presented individually were hypertension (29 %) and 
diabetes (24 %). Blood group “B” was the most frequent (42 %), followed by blood group “A” (35 %). A total of 87 patients (15.3 %) died

during the follow-up period. The total follow-up time was 7692 persondays, resulting in an incidence rate of 11.3 deaths per 1000 person-days 
of observation (95 % CI: 9.17–13.95). The Chi-square test showed a 
statistically significant difference in COVID-19-associated mortality 
across different patient characteristics. Mortality was higher among 
older adults compared to younger adults (44 % among ≥65 vs. 26 % 
among 18–40 age group). COVID-19-associated mortality was markedly 
higher among patients with both hypertension and diabetes (64 % vs. 
36 %) and among those with either hypertension or diabetes alone. 
However, no significant difference in mortality was observed across 
ABO blood groups (Table 1).
Comparison of COVID-19 severity with characteristics of patients
Half (50.53 %) and 23.68 % of the patients develop mild and severe 
COVID-19, respectively (Fig. 1).
A statistically significant difference in COVID-19 severity was 
observed across patient characteristics. Older adults (≥65 years) showed 
higher proportions of severe cases (10 %) compared to younger age 
groups (18–40: 7 %; 40–64: 8 %). Patients with comorbid hypertension 
and diabetes had more severe cases (9 %) than those without these 
conditions (6 % for hypertension alone, 5 % for diabetes alone). Blood 
group distribution revealed equal proportions of severe cases in groups 
A and B (9 % each), followed by O (4 %) and AB (2 %) (Table 2).
Multicollinearity test
Variance inflation factor (VIF) and tolerance were computed to 
check the existence of multicollinearity. A VIF above 4 or tolerance 
below 0.25 indicates multicollinearity might exist [30]. In this study, the 
maximum VIF was 1.21, with a mean VIF of 1.1, and the minimum 
tolerance value was 0.8. Thus, there is no multicollinearity between 
covariates.
Survival difference between ABO blood group
Kaplan-Meier survival curve and Log-rank test were computed to

determine the survival difference between blood types. The Cox proportional hazards model showed no significant association between 
blood group and survival. Compared to blood group A, blood group O 
had an AHR = 0.95 (95 % CI: 0.65–1.39), blood group B had an AHR =
0.92 (95 % CI: 0.58–1.46), and blood group AB had an AHR = 1.07 (95 
% CI: 0.63–1.82). (Fig. 2).

Association of ABO blood group with COVID-19 severity
To determine the association between ABO blood group and COVID19 severity, variables such as age, comorbidity, number of comorbidities, hypertension, and diabetes were included in a multivariable 
multinomial logistic regression model. The multivariable analysis (after 
adjustment) did not show any blood group to be significantly associated 
with COVID-19 severity (Table 3).
Association of ABO blood group with COVID-19 mortality
After adjusting (for age, comorbidity, hypertension, and diabetes), 
multivariate logistic regression analysis shows that ABO blood group is 
not significantly associated with COVID-19 mortality. (Table 4).
Discussion
The study aims to investigate the relationship between ABO blood

group with COVID-19 severity and mortality. The overall incidence of 
mortality was 11.3 deaths per 1000 person-days of observation. More 
than half of the patients (50.53 %) had mild COVID-19, followed by 
severe (23.68 %), asymptomatic (14.74 %), and moderate COVID-19. 
This study revealed no significant relationship between ABO blood 
group and COVID-19 severity and mortality.
Mild COVID-19 is found to be prevalent (23 %) in blood type B. 
Wearus’ severe COVID-19 is more prevalent (9.3 %) in blood group A. 
Among blood groups, less prevalent (1.6 %) severe COVID-19 is recorded in blood type AB. Moreover, COVID-19-associated mortality is 
found to be high in blood type A (7.4 %). However, no statistically 
significant association exists between ABO blood type and COVID-19 
severity or morality.
Different studies revealed different findings. A study done in Libya 
found that people with blood group A are more likely to develop severe 
disease, while the risk of developing severe COVID-19 is low in blood 
group O [31]. The above finding is also supported by other studies

[32,33]. On the other hand, a study done by Saudi Arabian concluded 
that blood group B is at risk for severe COVID-19 disease [34]. Moreover, another study found that individuals with blood group AB are 
linked to a higher risk of developing severe COVID-19 [12]. The major 
hypothesis includes: Furin levels may be lower in blood group O individuals, which would reduce the virus’ infectivity, and levels of Creactive protein and alkaline phosphatase may be higher in blood group 
A individuals than in blood group O individuals. Blood group O patients 
had natural anti-A and anti-B antibodies that may be partially protective 
against SARS-CoV-2 infection [35,36].
In contrast, our study disproves the above findings that there is no 
relation between ABO blood group and COVID-19 severity. Our results 
aligned with studies in the USA [20] and Turkey [37]. Moreover, the 
mortality risk is high in blood group A [32]. Another study conducted in 
India shows that blood group B is more likely to die from COVID-19 than 
other blood types [14]. Besides, further study found that the risk of 
death was slightly increased among type AB individuals [38]. 
Conversely, patients with type O blood had a decreased risk of death 
[39]. The possible hypothesis emerges that SARS-CoV-2 has ABO(H)- 
like structures in its envelope glycoproteins and could be asymmetrically transmitted due to a protective effect of the ABO antibodies, ABH 
antigens could enable SARS-CoV-2 interaction with the host’ cells; nonO blood type is associated with a higher risk of thromboembolism; and 
patients with blood type O at a lower risk for severe outcomes [40].
A study in Mexico revealed quite different findings, asserting that

patients with blood group A are less likely to die from COVID-19 than 
those with blood group O [16]. Those findings disagreed with our results, asserting no significant difference in COVID-19-associated mortality between ABO blood groups. Our findings are consistent with other 
studies done in India [41] and USA [42].
There is inconclusiveness in the findings of different studies. Thus, 
further exploration with a larger and well-controlled comparative study 
is recommended. The limitations of this study include the small sample 
size and the absence of data on Rhesus (Rh) factor and Duffy group 
differences, which could have helped determine possible associations 
with COVID-19 severity and mortality. The limited number of patients 
included in the study may also have affected the strength of the 
conclusions.
Conclusion
In conclusion, this study found no significant association between 
ABO blood group and COVID-19 severity and mortality. This is consistent with some other studies, but there are also studies that have found 
conflicting results. Therefore, further well-designed and controlled 
studies are needed to explore the potential link between ABO blood 
group and COVID-19 severity and mortality.
